title: Thaci Was Convicted at The Hague. Russia Used the Verdict to Attack NATO.
subtitle: The most politically invested audience left no trace in the corpus
body_md:
The Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague convicted former President Hashim Thaci of war crimes and crimes against humanity on September 16, sentencing him to 25 years in prison. Three other former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders received convictions on charges arising from the 1998-99 Kosovo war. The verdict produced sharply different reactions across Balkan political lines — Kosovo's political class denounced it as unjust, Serbia's government welcomed it as vindication — and drew procedural reports from Canada, Brazil, India, and Taiwan. One outlet turned it into something else entirely.

[RT](https://www.rt.com/news/645848-hashim-thaci-guilty-verdict/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=RSS) ran: "NATO-backed Kosovo separatist convicted of war crimes." Not "former Kosovo president," not "Kosovo Liberation Army leader," but "NATO-backed separatist" — framing Thaci as a Western proxy all along, and the Hague conviction as proof of a contradictory Western intervention: the alliance backed a criminal. RT also led with violent protests attacking the EU office in Kosovo and the Netherlands, foregrounding political instability over judicial process. No other outlet centred the protest violence. The verdict was a Hague accountability mechanism; RT made it a critique of NATO's Balkans legacy.

Global news coverage was otherwise factual and sparse. [Globe and Mail](https://www.theglobeandmail.com/world/article-kosovo-former-president-hashim-thaci-sentenced-war-crimes/) provided the headline event: "Hague court sentences Kosovo's former president Hashim Thaci to 25 years for war crimes. He was convicted of four counts of war crimes committed during his country's war for independence from Serbia." [RFE/RL](https://www.rferl.org/a/hague-court-former-kosovo-president-thaci-guilty-war-crimes/33857358.html) and Folha de São Paulo offered clean procedural accounts without engaging the political fallout.

[Balkan Insight](https://balkaninsight.com/2026/09/16/kosovo-slams-unjust-conviction-of-hashim-thaci-serbian-minister-applauds/btj/) — the closest thing to a regional specialist in this corpus — captured the domestic split directly: "Top politicians in Kosovo said the Hague judgment finding ex-President Thaci and three other Kosovo Liberation Army ex-leaders guilty of war crimes was unjust — but a Serbian minister said it proved the KLA was 'criminal'." Balkan Insight also reported uniquely on the parallel obstruction-of-justice sub-trial, in which Thaci's defence sought acquittal on grounds that witness-intimidation conversations never translated into actual intimidation — a legally distinct proceeding from the main war crimes case, absent from all other coverage.

[Deutsche Welle English](https://www.dw.com/en/serbian-president-vucic-criticizes-kosovo-war-crimes-verdict/a-79307654?maca=en-rss-en-all-1573-rdf) added the Serbia-side reaction: "The conviction of four former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders has drawn sharply different reactions across the Balkans. Serbia has accused the court of failing to fully address crimes against Serbs." Germany provided the broadest contextualization in Western-language coverage, running pieces in both English and German on the divergent Balkan reactions.

[The Hindu](https://www.thehindu.com/news/international/why-was-the-former-president-of-kosovo-convicted-by-the-hague-explained/article71475621.ece) was the only outlet to reach back to the 2010 Council of Europe Marty report, which alleged that the KLA placed Serbs in secret detention centres where they were subjected to inhuman treatment and "ultimately 'disappeared'." That background — the evidentiary basis that preceded the Hague proceedings by 16 years — appeared nowhere else. International coverage reported the outcome; only The Hindu supplied the pre-trial context.

The most structurally significant absence is Serbia. Despite Serbian President Vučić and at least one Serbian minister both commenting publicly on the verdict, no Serbian outlet appears in this corpus. The state most directly invested in the outcome as a historical and political matter — the state whose population constituted the victims named in the charges — is entirely absent from global coverage of the verdict's aftermath. The most politically loaded readings of what happened in The Hague are being made without the country that most wanted the result.
